summary:
Saudi Arabia has no codified penal code. Judges apply an uncodified interpretation of sharia drawn from the Quran and Sunnah, and same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity are prosecuted under that framework. Penalties range from fines and flogging through lengthy or indeterminate imprisonment to death in the most severe cases. Same-sex relations are illegal for men and women, and foreigners convicted of homosexual conduct face deportation in addition to corporal and custodial penalties.

Deviation from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence. Gender nonconformity is not merely evidence attached to another charge; police and morality-enforcement officers apply the provisions against gender-nonconforming people directly and with wide discretion. There is no legal gender recognition, no legal status for same-sex relationships, no discrimination protection, and LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

Enforcement is documented, and it is lethal. In April 2005, dozens of Saudi men arrested at a Jeddah party described in press coverage as a gay wedding, where they were said to have been dancing and behaving like women, were sentenced by a closed court without defence lawyers to a combined 14,200 lashes and up to two years in prison. In October 2021, five men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media. A Pakistani transgender woman, Mohammad Amin, died in Saudi custody after being rounded up with 34 others and held in Azizia prison in Riyadh; Pakistani activists and her family say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes, aggravating a chronic heart condition, while Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack. The dispute over the cause of death is unresolved.

Screening reaches travellers before they act on the ground. Entry and exit visa paperwork does not ask about sexual orientation, but it does ask nationality, sex, religion and marital status. Tourist visas were introduced in 2019 alongside a Public Decency Law that fines public displays of affection and immodest clothing. Work-visa applicants must pass an HIV test on arrival and again before permit renewal, and foreigners found to be infected are deported. Enforcement also reaches expression published abroad: Amnesty International documented a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 August 2024 as he was returning to the United Kingdom with his family, targeted for social media posts published before he had entered the country at all.

Official welcome messaging sits alongside the statute without changing it. In May 2023 the Saudi Tourism Authority's FAQ page was updated to state that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, are welcome, and VisitSaudi states that privacy will be respected. The United Kingdom's foreign travel advice notes that same-sex relations remain illegal, that legal action is uncommon, and that couples should avoid public affection; it states plainly that being transgender is not recognised, and warns that trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and with access to medical care. Access to care is a real constraint on the ground: the government has designated several hospitals to treat people with AIDS and HIV, but other hospitals often refuse such patients or treat them without compassion. Bars and nightclubs are illegal, public cinemas — permitted only since 2018 — have LGBTQ themes edited out of films, and customs maintains a banned list of films and television shows. A 2024/25 international LGBTQ+ risk map ranks Saudi Arabia among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers, alongside Somalia, Yemen, Uganda and Afghanistan.
tangentialFactors:
Risk rankings consistently place Saudi Arabia at the extreme end of the scale for LGBTQ travellers. The 2024/25 A3M Global Monitoring LGBTQ+ Risk Map groups it with Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, the United Arab Emirates, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan, a set of jurisdictions that share criminal statutes applied against gender and sexuality nonconformity.

The gap between tourism messaging and enforceable law is the single largest source of uncertainty for a visitor. The May 2023 statement that LGBTQ visitors are welcome and the foreign travel advice that legal action is uncommon are both sourced to authorities or to foreign governments assessing Saudi practice; neither has any bearing on the statutory position, which has not changed. In September 2013 Gulf states discussed a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners, which officials later downplayed as a mere proposal; no evidence in the record establishes that it was adopted.

Public space is heavily curated in ways a visitor will notice. Bars and nightclubs are illegal; cinemas, reopened only since 2018, carry edited prints; customs operates a banned list of films and television titles. Observers reported that MDLBeast Soundstorm, an annual multi-day music festival in Riyadh, included public display of LGBTQI+ culture, while appearing to support homosexuality can result in prosecution for individuals and for clubs alike. In June 2022 officials in Riyadh seized rainbow-colored products in a crackdown framed as curbing promotion of homosexuality.

The regime against gender nonconformity has a documented history of length. The April 2005 Jeddah sentences totalled 14,200 lashes across dozens of defendants, handed down in a closed trial without defence lawyers; a Human Rights Watch researcher described prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct as flagrant human rights violations. The pattern of arrests for cross-dressing on social media continued into the 2020s.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country, so no domestic civil-society machinery exists for residents seeking redress, documentation or community support.

Public education is required to teach Islamic values strongly condemning homosexuality. Ministry of Education textbooks stated that homosexuality is one of the most disgusting sins and greatest crimes, and prescribed capital punishment for public homosexual intercourse, though in 2020 the Ministry was found to have removed the death-penalty condemnation from textbooks. In 2012 the government asked the Commission for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice to help expel students judged to be gay or lesbian on the basis of their mannerisms and fashion taste. Private schools, which mainly serve expatriates, have discretion over curriculum covering homosexuality.

HIV prevention education for men who have sex with men is minimal, although a 2024 report by the national AIDS programme makes some mention of them. Condoms were until recently rarely available outside certain hospitals and medical supply stores. Residents as well as incoming workers are exposed to the HIV-testing requirement, which applies on arrival and before permit renewal.

The June 2022 seizure of rainbow-colored goods in Riyadh explicitly targeted the young generation, confiscating children's hair accessories, backpacks, pencil cases and rainbow-striped crayon packs. Gender-nonconforming residents face the same criminal provisions as visitors, as the October 2021 Northern Borders arrests illustrate: five men were detained for filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage online.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the record quantifies how many prosecutions for same-sex conduct or gender nonconformity are brought each year, so the foreign travel advice assessment that legal action is uncommon cannot be tested against case data. Whether arrest frequency has changed since the 2019 tourist-visa launch is unresolved.

The competing accounts of Mohammad Amin's death in custody remain unresolved. Pakistani activists and family members attribute the death to beatings that aggravated a heart condition; Saudi authorities attribute it to a heart attack. No independent forensic finding is available in the record.

Outcomes after sentencing are not sourced. Whether the 14,200 lashes and prison terms handed down in 2005 were carried out in full, and what followed the October 2021 cross-dressing arrests, are both unverified here.

The September 2013 proposal to test and ban gay foreigners was publicly downplayed by officials as a mere proposal. Its current legal status is not established by any source in the record, and it should not be treated as an operative screening measure.

No source establishes whether the 2023 tourism-authority welcome statement has any practical effect on enforcement decisions by police or the courts, or whether tourist-visa holders are subject to the HIV test that applies to work-visa applicants.
